subject: geography
prompt: What is **manufacturing**?

image.alt: Four rows showing a raw material, a factory and a finished product

options.text: Growing crops in large quantities on farms
Producing goods in large quantities by processing raw materials into more valuable products
Digging minerals out of the earth
Selling finished goods in a market

hint: Think of paper from wood or sugar from sugarcane.
explanation: **Manufacturing** is the production of goods in large quantities after processing raw materials into more valuable products, for example paper from wood, sugar from sugarcane, steel from iron ore and aluminium from bauxite. Growing crops and mining are primary activities, and selling is a service.

subject: geography
prompt: At a festival market, the shops sell shoes, clothes, utensils and diyas. Which item is made by individual artisans (craftspeople) in a **household industry**?

image.alt: Three cards: shoes and clothes, utensils and diyas, each with a question mark for who makes it

hint: Household industries are run by single artisans, not by big machines.
explanation: **Diyas** are made by individual artisans in household industry. Shoes, clothes and sugar come from machines in large industries, and some utensils come from small industries.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these are reasons why the manufacturing sector is called the **backbone of development**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Four cards: agriculture, jobs, exports and value of goods

options.text: It gives jobs in secondary and tertiary sectors, reducing dependence on farm income
Export of manufactured goods brings in foreign exchange
It keeps industry only in regions that are already developed

hint: One option makes agriculture disappear; another ignores backward areas.
explanation: Manufacturing modernises agriculture, creates jobs outside farming and earns **foreign exchange** through exports. It does **not** make agriculture unnecessary, because the two move hand in hand. Public sector and joint sector industries were also meant to **reduce regional disparities** by going to tribal and backward areas, so keeping industry only in developed regions is the opposite of the aim.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Farms send raw materials to agro-industries and receive pumps, fertilisers and tools

assertion: Agriculture and manufacturing industry move hand in hand (support each other).
reason: Agro-industries get their raw materials from farms. They also sell farmers items such as irrigation pumps, fertilisers, pesticides and pipes.
hint: Look at the arrows going both ways between the farms and the agro-industries.
explanation: Both statements are true and R explains A. Farms supply **raw materials** to agro-industries, while the industries supply **pumps, fertilisers, insecticides, pipes, machines and tools** that raise farm productivity. So the two sectors depend on each other.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these industries is **mineral-based**?

image.alt: Jute mill
Sugar mill
Cement industry
Cotton mill

hint: Mineral-based industries use minerals and metals as raw materials.
explanation: **Cement** uses limestone, silica and gypsum, so it is mineral-based. Jute, sugar and cotton industries use **agricultural** raw materials, so they are agro-based. Iron and steel, aluminium, machine tools and petrochemicals are other mineral-based examples.

image.alt: Four rows showing a raw material, a factory and a finished product

subject: geography
prompt: **Consumer industries** produce goods that people use directly. Which of these are consumer industries? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Cards: basic industries supply raw material to other factories; consumer industries make goods for direct use

hint: Basic industries supply other factories; consumer industries supply people.
explanation: **Sugar, toothpaste, fans** (also paper and sewing machines) are consumer industries. **Iron and steel, copper smelting and aluminium smelting** are basic or key industries because their products are raw materials for making other goods.

subject: geography
prompt: A small-scale industry is defined by the maximum investment allowed on its assets. At present, this limit is **₹1 crore**. The chart shows the investments of four units in ₹ lakh (1 crore = 100 lakh). How many of them are small-scale units?

image.alt: Bar chart of four units with a dashed line at the one crore limit

hint: Convert 1 crore into lakh before comparing with the bars.
explanation: 1 crore = 100 lakh, so units **A (40), B (75) and C (98)** are within the limit and only **D (130)** exceeds it: **three** small-scale units. Taking 1 crore as 10 lakh would give *none*, and ignoring the limit would give *all four*.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each industry with its **sector of ownership**.

image.alt: Four ownership cards

hint: Who owns it: the government, individuals, both together, or the producers themselves?
explanation: **BHEL and SAIL** are owned and run by government agencies (public sector). **Bajaj Auto Ltd** is owned by individuals (private sector). **OIL** is jointly owned by the public and private sectors (joint sector). The **coir industry in Kerala** is run by producers who pool resources and share profit or loss (cooperative sector).

subject: geography
prompt: Why does the textile industry hold a **unique position** (special place) in the Indian economy?

image.alt: Five bars rising in height showing value added along the textile chain

options.text: It is the only industry in the country that is self-reliant and complete in the value chain, from raw material to the highest value-added products
It uses no agricultural raw material at all
It imports all of its yarn from other countries
It is run only by the government

hint: Think about the whole chain from fibre to garment.
explanation: The textile industry contributes to industrial production, employment and foreign exchange, and it is the **only industry that is self-reliant and complete in the value chain**. It is closely linked with agriculture, so it does use farm raw material such as cotton.

subject: geography
prompt: Industries can be classified by the **bulk and weight** of their raw materials and finished goods. Which pair of industries is classified correctly in this way?

image.alt: A balance with steel beams on one side and electric bulbs on the other

options.text: Iron and steel: heavy industry; electrical goods: light industry
Iron and steel: light industry; electrical goods: heavy industry
Both iron and steel and electrical goods: heavy industries
Both iron and steel and electrical goods: light industries

hint: Which one needs heavy, bulky material and costly transport?
explanation: **Iron and steel** is a heavy industry, because its raw materials and finished goods are heavy and bulky. **Electrical goods** industries use light raw materials and make light goods, so they are light industries.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the stages of making a garment from **cotton** in the correct order.

image.alt: Five bars rising in height showing value added along the textile chain
Dyed fabric in a vat
Cotton plant
A shirt
A ball of yarn
Woven fabric

hint: The product after each stage: raw fibre, yarn, fabric, dyed fabric, garment.
explanation: Value is added step by step: **fibre production** gives raw fibre, **spinning** makes yarn, **weaving or knitting** makes fabric, **dyeing and finishing** colours it, and **garment manufacture** makes the final product.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the stage where cotton fibre is turned into **yarn**.

image.alt: A row of five stages of making clothes from cotton

hint: Yarn is made by twisting fibres, using a wheel.
explanation: **Spinning** turns raw fibre into yarn. The loom then weaves yarn into fabric, dyeing and finishing colour the fabric, and garment manufacture makes the shirt.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the machine on which **yarn is woven into fabric**.

image.alt: A row of five stages of making clothes from cotton

hint: Threads cross each other on this frame.
explanation: The **loom** weaves yarn into fabric. Weaving is done by handloom, powerloom and in mills, while spinning produces the yarn used by the loom.

subject: geography
prompt: Early cotton mills were concentrated in the cotton-growing belt of Maharashtra and Gujarat. Which of these was **not** a factor that helped this?

image.alt: Cards for raw material, market, transport, labour and climate

options.text: Market and transport, including accessible ports

hint: The text lists raw cotton, market, transport with ports, labour and one kind of climate.
explanation: Early mills grew where there was **raw cotton, a market, transport with port facilities, labour and a moist climate**. A dry, cold climate was not a factor; the text names a *moist* climate.

subject: geography
prompt: Which statement about **spinning and weaving** in the cotton textile industry is correct?

image.alt: Spinning mills grouped together while weaving looms are scattered

options.text: Weaving is concentrated in a few big mills, while spinning is scattered in homes
Spinning is concentrated in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu, while weaving is highly decentralised
Weaving makes world-class fabric using all the high-quality yarn produced
Both spinning and weaving are done only in large mills

hint: One stage is clustered in mills, the other is spread out to keep traditional skills alive.
explanation: **Spinning** continues to be centralised in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. **Weaving** is highly decentralised so that traditional skills and designs can be used, and it is done by handloom, powerloom and in mills. The text adds that weaving gives low-quality fabric because it cannot use much of the high-quality yarn.

subject: geography
prompt: At the time of Partition in 1947, **three-fourths** of the jute-producing area went to Bangladesh. What fraction of the jute-producing area stayed in India?

image.alt: Pie chart: three quarters of the jute-growing area went to Bangladesh

hint: Subtract three-fourths from the whole.
explanation: The whole area is 1, so what remained is $1-\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{4}$, i.e. **25%**. The jute **mills** stayed in India, but most of the growing area went to Bangladesh. Choosing 75% reports the share that left, and one-third misreads the ratio 3 : 1.

subject: geography
prompt: Select the factors responsible for the location of jute mills in the **Hugli basin**.

image.alt: Six cards of possible location factors for jute mills

options.text: Inexpensive water transport supported by rail and road
Cheap labour from West Bengal and nearby states
Abundant water for processing raw jute

hint: Think of the raw material, the river, the workers and the water.
explanation: Jute mills grew along the Hugli because of **nearby jute areas, cheap water transport with rail and road links, abundant water for processing and cheap labour**. Kolkata also provides banking, insurance and port facilities. Iron ore has nothing to do with jute.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange these events in the order in which they happened.

image.alt: Four icons for the first textile mill, first jute mill, first cement plant and Partition

items.text: Partition: three-fourths of the jute-growing area goes to Bangladesh
First cement plant set up in Chennai
First successful cotton textile mill set up in Mumbai
First jute mill set up at Rishra near Kolkata

hint: Three of these are first mills or plants dated 1854, 1855 and 1904.
explanation: The first successful cotton mill in **Mumbai** came in **1854**, the first jute mill at **Rishra** in **1855**, and the first cement plant in **Chennai** in **1904**. **Partition** followed in **1947**.

subject: geography
prompt: The sugar industry works only during the cane-crushing season. According to the text, which sector of ownership is it **ideally suited** to?

image.alt: Sugarcane field, a truck, a crushing mill and sacks of sugar

hint: Think about who could best run a mill that works only part of the year.
explanation: Because the industry is **seasonal**, it suits the **cooperative sector**, in which producers of the raw material pool resources and share profit or loss. Cooperatives are also more successful in the southern and western states.

subject: geography
prompt: Sugarcane is bulky. It loses sucrose (its sugar) while it is being carried (hauled). Tap the step where this loss happens.

image.alt: Sugarcane field, a truck carrying cane, a crushing mill and sacks of sugar

hint: Loss happens while the cane is on the move.
explanation: In **haulage**, the cane's sucrose content falls. That is why sugar mills are located close to the cane fields.

subject: geography
prompt: Sixty per cent of the sugar mills are in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Out of every **20 mills**, how many are in the other states?

image.alt: Pie chart: sixty percent of sugar mills in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar

hint: Find 40% of 20.
explanation: The other states hold $100\%-60\%=40\%$ of the mills, and $\frac{40}{100}\times 20 = 8$. Giving 12 counts the mills of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, 40 reads the percentage as a number, and 10 assumes an equal split.

subject: geography
prompt: Which statement about India's position in the world is correct, according to the chapter?

image.alt: A podium with sugarcane, a sack and a jute bale

options.text: India is the largest producer of sugar and second in gur and khandsari
India is second to Bangladesh in producing raw jute
India is first in exporting jute goods
India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods and is second to Bangladesh as an exporter

hint: One chapter fact is about jute; the sugar rank is the other way round.
explanation: India is **first in production of raw jute and jute goods**, but **second to Bangladesh as an exporter**. In sugar India is **second** in the world, while in **gur and khandsari** it is **first**, so the sugar statement reverses the ranks.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Pictures of a bridge, car, tools, an aircraft, containers and gears

assertion: Iron and steel is called a heavy industry.
reason: Its raw materials and finished goods are heavy and bulky, which means heavy transportation costs.
hint: Think about moving iron ore, coal and steel sheets.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are heavy and so are the finished goods, so transport is costly. Iron and steel is also a **basic industry**, since every other industry depends on it for machinery, and its production and consumption are regarded as an index of a country's development.

subject: geography
prompt: Iron ore, coking coal and limestone are needed in the ratio of about **4 : 2 : 1**. A plant uses 28 tonnes of iron ore. How much **limestone** does it need?

image.alt: Bars in the ratio 4 to 2 to 1 for iron ore, coking coal and limestone

hint: One part of the ratio equals 28 divided by 4.
explanation: One part is $28\div 4 = 7$ tonnes, so limestone (1 part) = **7 tonnes** and coking coal (2 parts) = 14 tonnes. Giving 14 tonnes quotes the coal, 4 tonnes divides 28 by the sum of the parts (7), and 56 multiplies the 28 tonnes by 2 instead of dividing by 4.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the place where **iron ore is melted**. Here, limestone is used as the fluxing material and coke is burned to heat the ore.

image.alt: A steel plant from raw material transport to rolling mill

hint: It is a tall furnace with a fire at its base.
explanation: In the **blast furnace**, iron ore is melted, limestone acts as flux, slag is removed and coke is burned to supply heat. The molten metal then goes to the moulds for pig iron.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the stage where steel is **rolled, pressed, cast or forged** into shape.

image.alt: A steel plant from raw material transport to rolling mill

hint: Think of rollers pressing metal into sheets.
explanation: **Shaping metal** is the last stage, by rolling, pressing, casting and forging. Before it, pig iron is purified in steel making.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the stages of manufacturing steel in order.

image.alt: Pictures of a bridge, car, tools, an aircraft, containers and gears

items.text: Shaping metal by rolling, pressing, casting and forging
Blast furnace: ore melted, limestone added, slag removed
Steel making: pig iron purified and manganese, nickel, chromium added
Transport of raw material to the plant
Pig iron: molten metal poured into moulds

hint: Raw material arrives first; shaping gives the final product.
explanation: Raw material is **transported** to the plant, melted in the **blast furnace**, poured into moulds as **pig iron**, purified in **steel making**, and finally **shaped** by rolling, pressing, casting and forging.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each stage of making steel with what happens in it.

image.alt: Cards for the four stages of making steel

right.text: Pig iron is purified by melting and oxidising impurities; manganese, nickel and chromium are added
Iron ore is melted, limestone acts as flux and slag is removed
Molten material is poured into moulds called pigs

hint: Follow the order of the flow chart: furnace, moulds, purification, shaping.
explanation: In the **blast furnace** ore is melted with limestone flux. **Pig iron** is molten metal poured into moulds called pigs. In **steel making** pig iron is purified and alloying metals are added. **Shaping metal** uses rolling, pressing, casting and forging.

subject: geography
prompt: Which are **properties of aluminium** mentioned in the chapter? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Cards on aluminium: weight, corrosion, heat, shaping, aircraft, utensils and wires

options.text: It becomes strong when mixed with other metals
It is a poor conductor of heat

hint: Aircraft makers choose it for a reason.
explanation: Aluminium is **light, resistant to corrosion, a good conductor of heat, malleable and strong when mixed with other metals**, so it is used for aircraft, utensils and wires. It is not heavy and brittle, and it conducts heat well.

subject: geography
prompt: About **4 to 6 tonnes of bauxite** give 2 tonnes of alumina. These 2 tonnes of alumina give **1 tonne of aluminium**. How much bauxite is needed for **5 tonnes of aluminium**?

image.alt: Bars drawn to scale: bauxite, alumina and aluminium

hint: The bauxite figure is for each tonne of aluminium.
explanation: For 1 tonne of aluminium the bauxite is 4 to 6 tonnes, so for 5 tonnes it is $5\times4=20$ to $5\times6=30$ tonnes. The option 4 to 6 tonnes forgets to scale; 10 tonnes is the alumina needed ($5\times2$); 8 to 12 tonnes multiplies the bauxite range by 2 instead of 5.

subject: geography
prompt: A regular supply of **electricity** is a main factor in deciding where to set up an aluminium smelter. Tap the part of the picture that stands for the electricity supply.

image.alt: A bauxite pile, a ship, an alumina refinery, a smelter and an electricity pylon

hint: Which structure carries power along wires?
explanation: The **electricity pylon** shows the power supply. Regular electricity and an assured, low-cost supply of raw material are the **two prime location factors** for aluminium smelters.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A bauxite pile, a ship, an alumina refinery, a smelter and an electricity pylon

assertion: Aluminium smelters are located where a regular supply of electricity is assured.
reason: Electricity is a major input at the smelting stage, where alumina is turned into aluminium.
hint: The flow chart of aluminium making shows electricity entering at the smelter.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. In the flow chart electricity goes to the **aluminium smelter** (with cryolite as an electrolyte), so plants are located where power is regular. The second prime factor is an assured source of bauxite at minimum cost.

subject: geography
prompt: The **Chhotanagpur plateau region** has the largest number of iron and steel industries. Which set of advantages explains why?

image.alt: Cards for iron ore, raw materials, labour and market

options.text: Low-cost iron ore, high-grade raw materials nearby, cheap labour and growth potential in the home market
Heavy rainfall, thick forests and a warm coast
Large oil reserves, cold climate and nearness to the sea
Cheap imported coal, a small market and costly labour

hint: Think of raw materials, workers and customers.
explanation: The region offers **low-cost iron ore, high-grade raw materials in proximity, cheap labour and vast growth potential in the home market**. The other sets name features that the text does not give as reasons.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each chemical with what the chapter says about it.

image.alt: Four cards showing chemical industry products

right.text: Used to make glass, soaps and detergents, and paper
Raw material for synthetic fibres, synthetic rubber, plastics, dye-stuffs and drugs
Entirely imported because there are no commercially usable reserves
Used to make fertilizers, synthetic fibres, plastics, adhesives, paints and dyes

hint: Inorganic chemicals come first; potash is a fertilizer nutrient.
explanation: **Sulphuric acid** is used for fertilizers, synthetic fibres, plastics, adhesives, paints and dyes. **Soda ash** goes into glass, soaps, detergents and paper. **Petrochemicals** (organic) are used for synthetic fibres, rubber, plastics, dyes and drugs. **Potash** is entirely imported.

subject: geography
prompt: Where are the plants of the **organic chemical** industry usually located?

image.alt: A refinery with a pipeline to a plant

options.text: Near oil refineries or petrochemical plants

hint: Organic chemicals such as petrochemicals come from refinery products.
explanation: Organic chemical plants are located **near oil refineries or petrochemical plants**, which supply their raw material. Inorganic chemical industries, in contrast, are widely spread over the country.

subject: geography
prompt: Complex fertilisers combine nitrogen (N), phosphate (P) and potash (K). Which of these is **entirely imported**, and why?

image.alt: Three fertiliser sacks marked N, P and K

options.text: Nitrogen, because India has no urea plants
Phosphate, because DAP cannot be made in India
Potash, because India has no commercially usable reserves of potash
Potash, because it is cheaper to import than to grow

hint: Think of the nutrient for which India has no reserves.
explanation: **Potash** is entirely imported since the country has no reserves of commercially usable potash or potassium compounds. India produces nitrogenous fertilisers (mainly urea) and phosphatic fertilisers such as DAP.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these is **not** a raw material or main input of the cement industry?

image.alt: Cards for three raw materials, coal, power and transport

hint: Bauxite belongs to a different metal industry.
explanation: Cement needs bulky and heavy raw materials such as **limestone, silica and gypsum**, plus coal, electric power and rail transport. **Bauxite** is the raw material of aluminium smelting.

subject: geography
prompt: After **liberalisation**, the demand for vehicles went up and the automobile industry grew well. What caused this?

image.alt: Pictures of a car, a bus, a truck and a two-wheeler

options.text: The coming in of new and contemporary models
A ban on new car models
A fall in the number of vehicle centres

hint: Think of what new customers could suddenly choose from.
explanation: After liberalisation, **new and contemporary models** stimulated demand, which led to healthy growth including passenger cars and two- and three-wheelers.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these is a product of the **electronics industry**?

image.alt: Sack of cement
Computer
Roll of steel
Bricks

hint: Transistor sets, televisions and telephones belong to this industry.
explanation: **Computers** are part of the electronics and IT industry, which also makes transistor sets, televisions, telephones, cellular telecom and radars. Bengaluru has emerged as the electronic capital of India, and the industry has greatly increased employment.

subject: geography
prompt: Match each picture with the **cause** of that type of pollution.

image.alt: A factory with a chimney, two pipes into a river, a generator and a waste heap
Cloud above a factory
A pipe discharging into water
A waste heap
A loudspeaker and an ear

right.text: Dumped glass, chemicals and garbage that make soil useless
Generators, drills and machinery making unwanted sound
Sulphur dioxide, carbon monoxide and smoke from factories
Dyes, acids, salts and heavy metals discharged into rivers

hint: Cloud and chimney, a pipe and water, a waste heap, a loudspeaker.
explanation: Picture 1 is **air pollution** (gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide, and smoke). Picture 2 is **water pollution** from effluents with dyes, acids, salts and heavy metals. Picture 3 is **land pollution** from dumped glass, chemicals and garbage. Picture 4 is **noise pollution** from generators, drills and machinery.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the source of **air pollution** in this scene.

image.alt: A factory with a smoking chimney, discharge pipes into a river, a noisy generator and a waste heap

hint: Air pollution comes from gases and smoke.
explanation: Smoke from the **chimney** carries gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide and particles like dust and mist. Chemical and paper factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants are among the sources.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap where **thermal pollution** of water is happening.

image.alt: A factory with a smoking chimney, discharge pipes into a river, a noisy generator and a waste heap

hint: Look for steam rising from water that is being drained.
explanation: **Thermal pollution** occurs when hot water from factories and thermal plants is drained into rivers and ponds before cooling. The steaming pipe shows this, while the other pipe carries chemical effluents (water pollution).

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the source of **noise pollution**.

image.alt: A factory with a smoking chimney, discharge pipes into a river, a noisy generator and a waste heap

hint: The sound waves are drawn next to it.
explanation: **Generators**, machinery, saws and drills make unwanted sound. Noise irritates, causes stress and can cause hearing impairment and raised heart rate and blood pressure.

subject: geography
prompt: Some industries are the **main culprits** of water pollution because they release their wastes into rivers. Which of these are they? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A factory with a smoking chimney, discharge pipes into a river, a noisy generator and a waste heap

hint: They release dyes, acids, salts or heavy metals.
explanation: The text names **paper, pulp, chemical, textile and dyeing, petroleum refineries, tanneries and electroplating** industries as the main culprits. Software parks and home handlooms are not listed.

subject: geography
prompt: Every litre of waste water discharged by industry pollutes **eight times** the quantity of fresh water. A factory discharges **25 litres**. How much fresh water is polluted?

image.alt: One drop of waste water becomes eight drops of polluted fresh water

hint: Multiply the discharge by eight.
explanation: $25\times 8 = 200$ litres. Adding 8 to 25 (33) mixes up 'times' with 'plus', 25 forgets the multiplier, and dividing by 8 gives about 3.

subject: geography
prompt: Arrange the three phases of **treating industrial effluents** in order.

image.alt: A factory with a smoking chimney, discharge pipes into a river, a noisy generator and a waste heap

items.text: Tertiary treatment by biological, chemical and physical processes, including recycling
Primary treatment by mechanical means such as screening, grinding and sedimentation
Secondary treatment by a biological process

hint: The mechanical phase comes first and recycling comes last.
explanation: **Primary** treatment is mechanical (screening, grinding, flocculation and sedimentation), **secondary** treatment is biological, and **tertiary** treatment uses biological, chemical and physical processes and includes recycling of waste water.

subject: geography
prompt: Tap the tank where **secondary treatment** of effluents (waste water) takes place by a biological process.

image.alt: A treatment plant with a screen tank, a tank with microbes, a filter and a return pipe

hint: Microbes are at work in this tank.
explanation: **Secondary treatment** is a biological process, shown by the tank with microbes. The first tank stands for mechanical (primary) treatment, and the filter with the pipe returning water to the factory stands for tertiary treatment and recycling.

subject: geography
prompt: Which of these are **suggested ways** to reduce industrial pollution? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Cards for air, water, rain and noise

options.text: Reuse and recycle water in two or more stages
Harvest rainwater to meet water needs
Use coal instead of oil or gas to reduce smoke
Release hot effluents straight into rivers
Fit smoke stacks with electrostatic precipitators and scrubbers

hint: Two options make pollution worse.
explanation: Water can be reused and recycled, rainwater harvested, generators fitted with **silencers**, and smoke stacks fitted with **electrostatic precipitators, fabric filters, scrubbers and inertial separators**. Smoke is reduced by using **oil or gas instead of coal**, so the coal option is reversed, and hot water must be **treated before** release into rivers.

subject: geography
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Rain falling on a waste heap and seeping down to groundwater

assertion: Soil pollution and water pollution are closely related.
reason: Rain water seeps (percolates) through polluted soil and carries the pollutants to the ground water.
hint: Follow the arrows from the rain to the groundwater.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Wastes such as glass, chemicals, effluents, salts and garbage make soil useless, and rain water carries the pollutants down so that **ground water also gets contaminated**.

subject: geography
prompt: NTPC has ISO 14001 certification for its Environment Management System. Which of these measures does the chapter list for it?

image.alt: Cards for trees, ash, equipment and monitoring

options.text: Providing green belts and managing ash ponds and recycling ash water

hint: The measures aim to keep ecological balance.
explanation: The chapter lists optimum use of equipment, **minimising waste by using ash, green belts for ecological balance and afforestation, ash pond management and ash water recycling**, and ecological monitoring with an on-line database. It stresses that sustainable development needs economic growth to be integrated with environmental concerns.
